newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-JOHNSON JOINS CRITICS OF REDUCED DOPING BANS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-JOHNSON JOINS CRITICS OF REDUCED DOPING BANS.

text.p: Michael Johnson added his voice on Saturday to the critics of the world governing body's decision to reduce bans for drug cheats.
"I disagree with it," said double Olympic champion Johnson, who starts the defence of his 400 metres world title here on Sunday. "The four-year ban was much more effective."
On Thursday, the International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) congress voted to halve the ban for serious drugs offences from four to two years because of difficulties with the civil courts.
"What I liked about the four-year ban is that it meant you missed an Olympics," Johnson said. "Now, you could be banned and still make it to the next Olympics."
Olympic and world high hurdles champion Allen Johnson and former Olympic and world 100 champion Linford Christie have already spoken out against the decision.
"It's a step backwards," said Johnson. "It puts us back where other sports are and our sport will probably be criticised for softening its position."
Johnson, the Olympic 200 and 400 metres champion, nearly missed the world championships after injury forced him out of the United States trials in June, which cost him his place in the U.S. team.
But the IAAF, eager to have the top athletes competing in Athens, brought in a controversial new rule, delivering automatic wild card entry to the defending champions.
Johnson, who completed the 200-400 double at the 1995 world championships, said he had ruled out a double here.

"At the beginning of the season, I decided I would not double here," he said. "I'll probably do it again, maybe at the next world championships (in 1999 in Seville, Spain) or at the 2000 Olympics (in Sydney)."
Johnson said he had fully recovered from the quadriceps injury he suffered during his head-to-head 150 metres race against Donovan Bailey in Toronto two months ago.
"I'm 100 percent fit and that all it takes for me to be 100 percent confident," he said. "If I didn't feel that way, I wouldn't be here."

When asked for his position on the debate on the world's fastest man, he said nobody would ever have the answer. He also brushed aside speculations that he might run the 100 metres or even the 800 in the future.

"I'm a 200 and 400 metres runner," he said. "Those are the events I like to watch and I like to compete in. That's what I'll be doing until the end of my career. I'm not a 100 metres runner and I'm not a 800 metres runner either."

Providing he is back at his brilliant best, many believe Johnson, who sent the 200 metres world record spinning into another dimension by clocking 19.32 seconds in Atlanta, could break fellow American Butch Reynold's 400 metres mark of 43.29 set nine years ago.
But he said that was not on his mind.
"I'm here to win and race as fast as I can," he said. "I'll look at the clock afterwards. I'm not here to break a world record."
